I had this long lecture that I developed about post-apocalyptic literature, about pandemics and Shakespeare and all themes that dovetailed with Station Eleven.

I was literally traveling the country delivering a lecture that contained the phrase, “There will always be another pandemic.” It is so embarrassing how shocked I was that there was, in fact, another pandemic. I was scrambling for toilet paper like everybody else.

Yeah, you're like, “Guys, I don’t know if you should put Clorox all over your groceries.”

Yeah. And I did.

I definitely did that, for probably longer than I should have.

Same.

I'm curious about how you deal with celebrity. Just thinking about that social media onslaught during Covid. You don't strike me as someone who's particularly eager to post, you know what I mean?

You've discovered my secret. I’m not eager to post.

How do you deal with that part of the job? And do you feel pressure to do it differently than you’re inclined to do?

If I were on Instagram just to be on Instagram, I don’t know if you’d ever see my face, you know? Because I love posting weird, beautiful little videos. Like, I just posted one that’s spiderwebs on a hiking trail in the Adirondacks last week.

If I see something cool and beautiful and I think, “Oh, that's kind of amazing,” in just a tiny little moment, and could I set it to music? That would be cool. I really like Reels. That’s how I probably naturally would use it. I do feel a certain pressure to post, I guess, to post my face for the algorithms. I do feel like I need to promote my books because it is literally how I pay my rent.

It just kind of feels like part of the job. I don't want to get too negative here because I do genuinely love interacting with readers. So I guess I kind of want it both ways.

There is pressure there. I find social media generally terrifying. I’ve had a lot of very negative interactions over the years, and what’s funny is just the way the human brain is wired, the positive interactions outweigh the negative interactions 1,000-to-one. But I also remember the negative ones. The negative ones stand out.

What is it like to promote a book in the year 2026? How has it changed?

I think that I have a very atypical experience of book promotion, because I had these three novels published by a really small press, and then I jumped to Knopf in the US, HarperCollins Canada, and Pan Macmillan in the UK for Station Eleven, and I've been with those three publishers ever since.

Because Station Eleven was so successful, a lot of marketing resources have been poured into the subsequent books. I think that that gives me a really unusual experience, and I think that it’s not normal at all. So it makes me hesitant to draw any generalizations, because for me it’s fine, you know?

But that’s certainly not the case for the vast majority of novelists. I think there's so much distraction and chatter and such short attention spans that I think it's incredibly difficult to start out as a novelist now. It was never actually easy, but my sense is that it might be harder now in this more fractured and more chaotic media landscape. I think it becomes harder for a novelist to break through.

Do you have any advice for those people?

Stay off Threads, for real. I don’t really post, but I do read. I see the most deranged publishing advice on Threads.

Like what?

I don't even know. Every time I read it, I’m like, “No, that makes no sense. Don't do that.”

I want to end by coming back to Exit Party. [As you said], you were accused, for lack of a better word, of being a prophet when Station Eleven came out before the Covid-19 pandemic. You've now written a book that is close to what we are going through in the US. Are you bracing yourself for a similar reaction?

Yeah. But look, if the country collapses, it’s not my fault.

She said it here first.

I didn’t do it. I just read the news and got freaked out like everybody else.

Is there anything in the worlds you’ve created in the book that you hope turns out to be prophetic?

Absolutely. I don’t want to take credit for the parties after … but you know what? It's hope itself. There is a lot of hope in this book. It opens at a moment when the country has collapsed, but something new is taking its place, and it's a kind of chaotic in-between period, but I never meant to imply that would last forever.

I think that settles down into something more stable and potentially better. And then on the side of the book that deals with a totalitarian state, that totalitarianism is already crumbling toward the end. I think that we see that even now in our current incredibly dark political moment.

I mean, maybe what you’ll get credit for predicting is the dawn of an even better version of this country.

That would be lovely.

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

entries.title: A New Headset to Help With Depression Is Now Available in the US
entries.summary: The device made by Flow Neuroscience is approved by the FDA and could help people get off antidepressants—but it costs $2,200.
entries.content:
An at-home wearable for the treatment of depression is now available by prescription in the US.

With roughly one in six American adults taking an antidepressant medication, Swedish firm Flow Neuroscience is positioning its device as an alternative to traditional drugs. But at the current four-figure price tag, it might take a while for the futuristic-looking headset to catch on with patients.

Worn on the forehead for 30 minutes a day and operated with an app, the device provides low-intensity electrical stimulation to the left frontal lobe of the brain, an area involved in regulating mood and emotions. People with depression tend to have lower activity and weaker neural connections in that part of the brain.

Flow received approval from the Food and Drug Administration last December, and its device is among a new breed of wearables that monitor, record from, or stimulate the brain. California-based Cognixion, for instance, has modified the Apple Vision Pro to build a communication system for paralyzed people that doesn’t depend on speech or motor control. A headband by Muse promises to improve meditation, and a device by Elemind is meant to help people fall asleep faster.

The Flow device targets the same part of the brain as transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, an approved treatment for depression that uses magnetic fields to activate neurons. With TMS, patients have to go to a clinic, and a full dosing series typically requires treatment sessions administered five days a week over several weeks. The whole course of treatment can cost up to $15,000 without insurance.

Flow CEO Daniel Månsson, a clinical psychologist before he cofounded the company, says he set out to make a more convenient option for patients. “In order to have a real impact on the problem, you need to create something that has the effect on the brain needed, but that can be used in a home environment in a safe and effective way,” he says.

In a trial of 174 people with major depressive disorder, 45 percent of participants who received Flow’s device experienced a remission in symptoms at 10 weeks compared to 22 percent of those in a control group who received a sham version. The trial included people who were taking antidepressants and those who weren’t—evidence that the device can, under medical supervision, be used in addition to medication, Månsson says.

Reported side effects were mild: Some people experienced skin irritation, headaches, and trouble concentrating. Antidepressants, meanwhile, can cause nausea, weight gain, drowsiness, dry mouth, and sexual problems, but these can go away a few weeks after beginning medication.

In Europe, where the device has been approved since 2019, more than 65,000 people have used the Flow device, says Månsson. The UK’s National Health Service is also piloting the headset.

In the US, patients will be able to get a prescription for the Flow device from a clinician in person or via telehealth. But at least for now, they’ll have to pay out of pocket to use it: $2,200 for 10 weeks and then $325 per month after. That’s a lot more than standard antidepressants, which are usually covered by insurance. Månsson says the company is working to get reimbursement from insurers.

Vinod Khosla, a billionaire venture capitalist and an early investor in Flow, thinks a nonchemical approach to treating depression is the way of the future. “My bet is, if you ask any person who's on depression drugs, they'd prefer not to be on them,” he says. “They'd like a nondrug, nonchemical treatment for it.”

entries.title: System 76 Pangolin Pro Review (2026): Powerhouse Linux Laptop
entries.summary: The System76 Pangolin Pro Linux Laptop wraps a speedy processor, plenty of ports, and a great operating system in a svelte, 16-inch package.
entries.content:
I have similar feelings about the very large glass trackpad. For things like photo editing, the trackpad's size is great, but I found my palms occasionally clicked the buttons at the bottom of the trackpad when I took a break from typing. It didn't happen often, but I learned to be careful about where I put my palms.

The 2-MP 1080p webcam is fine for casual use, chatting with family and friends, but if you do a lot of Zoom meetings in a professional context, you may want an external webcam. Also, open-source purists should note that Coreboot still does not support AMD Ryzen chips (or AMD does not support Coreboot, depending on how you want to look at it), so the Pangolin Pro does not use open firmware.

Finally, the Pangolin Pro is easy to open up to replace or repair components. There are nine screws on the bottom of the chassis, and none of them are hidden under the rubber feet or other shenanigans. Unscrew them all, and the bottom lifts off, giving you access to the SSD slots, RAM, WiFi card, and the rest of the internals. You'll have no trouble upgrading components down the road if you decide to, say, upgrade your memory when RAM prices come back down. (Is that actually going to happen? Who knows.)

Pop!_OS Linux Integration

System76's Pop!_OS Linux has long provided what I consider one of the best Linux experiences out there. The Cosmic Desktop and the custom apps System76 ships with it provide that "just works" stability you need to use Linux daily without even noticing you're using Linux.

As a long-time Linux user, I'm probably biased, but I find Linux to offer a better user experience than MacOS or Windows. I never feel like I'm fighting the operating system to get things the way I want them. I mainly run a terminal for writing, email, reading RSS feeds, etc, and a web browser. When I need to edit photos, I open Darktable; videos in DaVinci Resolve. None of that should require much from an operating system, but for some reason it's all easier for me in Linux.

Pop!_OS is particularly good in this regard, as it manages to feel familiar enough for Linux newcomers to find their way around, while still offering a good amount of power-user features. For instance, if you don't know what tiling windows are, you never need to be bothered about them, but if you want them, you can enable them with a toggle switch in the settings app. There are loads of (customizable) keyboard shortcuts for developers who eschew the mouse, and there are plenty of trackpad gestures to control workspaces, window focus, and more.

Should You Buy It?

At the beginning, I said the Pangolin Pro is overkill for most peoples needs, which is true. Although the Pangolin is actually cheaper than the smaller System76 Lemur Pro (review coming soon), the more portable Lemur Pro might be a better fit for many. However, if you're doing highly intensive things with your laptop, building local AI models or training custom agents, compiling software, or just want a powerful, future-proof machine, Pangolin is one of the best Linux laptops I've tested.

If you're a Linux user looking for a 16-inch laptop with all the bells and whistles, and one that isn't crazy expensive or crazy heavy, this is the machine I would get.

entries.title: The Supreme Court Just Blocked Trump’s Efforts to Control Mail-In Voting for the Midterms
entries.summary: The ruling bars the United States Postal Service from implementing restrictions that experts and election officials say would upend voting in November.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration’s bid to impose severe restrictions on mail-in voting just weeks ahead of the midterms.

The court, which was divided 7-2, with conservative justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissenting, upheld a lower court’s injunction blocking the United States Postal Service from implementing new rules around who can receive a mail-in ballot ahead of November’s vote.

Under this new rule, states would have had to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service, which would then confirm that ballots were sent only to people on that list. The USPS does not typically hold such a role.

“The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction,” Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson.

Kavanaugh did add, however, that “there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority. But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious … because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”

Voting by mail has also already begun in some states ahead of November’s elections, making the implementation of this plan even more difficult for Americans across the country to vote.

This is a major loss for President Donald Trump, who has long railed against mail-in voting, claiming without evidence that it led to election fraud, and the latest legal defeat the president and his administration have faced in a multipronged approach to undermine trust in US elections.

The White House and the USPS did not respond to a request for comment about the ruling.

“Today, Donald Trump lost another battle in his unconstitutional war to choose his own voters, and the American people are winners,” Cisco Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state, wrote in an emailed statement. “This ruling affirms what our Constitution has always held: Elections belong to the American people, not a desperate man in Washington. Democratic secretaries of state applaud the court on upholding this fundamental principle, and we stand ready to fight any attempt to cause chaos, fear, and intimidation in our elections.”

The mail-in voting battle has occurred since the spring, when the president signed an executive order in March titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.” The order demanded that all states send the Postal Service a list of voters who would receive mail-in ballots. In turn, the USPS could refuse to deliver ballots to voters not on the lists or ballots that didn’t comply with new rules around barcodes and envelopes.

The majority of the provisions of the executive order were quickly blocked by federal courts before the Trump administration appealed the rulings to the Supreme Court in July. Last month, the conservative court ruled along ideological lines to allow the new rules to proceed, writing that the states that sought to block the rules didn’t have standing because the rules hadn’t been implemented yet.

In the wake of the ruling, a USPS whistleblower claimed that the online portal for the new rules had been hastily thrown together without the necessary care and attention needed for such a critical piece of software.

“The whistleblower’s allegations make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement the [executive order’s] provisions in a way that safeguards every citizen’s right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections,” Senator Richard Blumenthal, who disclosed the whistleblower's warning, wrote in a letter to the postmaster general. “Despite this, the Trump administration appears intent on USPS moving forward with its flawed plans, no matter the chaos they may create.”

entries.title: The Top New Features in Apple’s iOS 27 and iPadOS 27
entries.summary: The latest iPhone update is chock-full of smart upgrades, with a big focus on improvements to Siri.
entries.content:
Apple's latest iPhone and iPad software—iOS 27 and iPadOS 27—is here. While this release won’t make as big of a splash as Apple’s big Liquid Glass redesign in the prior version, there's still plenty here that could change how you use your device.

iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 focus largely on stability improvements that you’ll notice in your everyday use. There are several quality-of-life improvements, like how Shortcuts are significantly easier to set up, but the big highlight is the Siri AI upgrade. Here's everything you need to know.

Updated September 14, 2026: We've refreshed this story to reflect the latest updates and that iOS and iPadOS 27 are rolling out today.

Is Your iPhone or iPad Compatible?

Apple sometimes drops a few older devices from the support list with new versions of its operating systems, supposedly because the aging hardware can’t run the latest screen behaviors without feeling sluggish. (Apple typically supports iPhones and iPads for six to seven years.) But there's good news this year. iPhones from 2019 and newer—the iPhone 11 and up, including the iPhone SE (2nd Gen)—will support iOS 27.

That means any iPhone that received iOS 26 is still compatible with iOS 27. If you're unsure of your iPhone model, go to Settings > General > About and look at the model name.

iPads aren't as straightforward, as they have a unique naming structure. Apple retired the “generations” moniker and is now using the chipset to denote the iPad model. You can check your iPad model using Apple’s support documentation. A few iPads are cut off from the iPadOS 27 update, including the 8th-gen iPad from 2020 and the 5th-gen iPad Mini.

  • iPad: 9th gen and later, including A16
  • iPad Mini: 6th gen and later, including A17 Pro
  • iPad Air 11-inch: 4th gen and later, including M2, M3, and M4
  • iPad Air 13-inch: M2 and later
  • iPad Pro 11-inch: 2nd gen and later
  • iPad Pro 12.9-inch: 4th gen and later
  • iPad Pro: M4 and later

How to Install iOS 27 or iPadOS 27

The final versions of iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 are here. Before installing, it’s very important that you back up your devices. Head to Settings, tap your name at the top, and select iCloud. Then tap iCloud Backup, and tap Back Up Now. Read our How to Back Up Your iPhone or iPad guide for other methods and more details.

Then, head to Settings > General > Software Update and choose iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 when you see the option. Installation will take several minutes, and your iPhone or iPad will restart, so set aside several minutes for the whole process.

Siri AI, the new assistant, will ask to index your phone or iPad to learn more about you, your apps, and your data so it can be more helpful. This indexing takes a while—anywhere from a few hours to a couple of days—so be prepared to wait a bit.

Apple Intelligence Only Works on Select iPhones

Remember—even if older iPhones and iPads receive the iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 update, that doesn't mean all of the new features will be available. Apple Intelligence is still only compatible with the iPhone 15 Pro and newer and select iPads, meaning that several artificial intelligence features are unavailable on older devices.

Top New iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 Features

Here's a top-line view of some of the biggest changes coming to iOS and iPadOS 27. The updates are largely the same across both operating systems.

Siri is finally becoming “a more capable assistant,” or so Apple claims. The company says this is largely thanks to its third-generation foundation models, developed from the ground up with Google's Gemini models. However, Apple says it isn't using Google's infrastructure to power Siri interactions and that no user data from Siri actions gets shared with Google.

Siri AI has an all-new look when you activate the assistant. It now resembles a glass orb. You can type or talk naturally to Siri, and there's even a dedicated Siri app where you can revisit previous conversations or pick up where you left off on a different device. Siri is also now in the camera app, giving you a more direct way to start a visual search, much like Google Lens. You can even point the camera at a restaurant bill, and Siri can split the tab between you and your friends.

The assistant understands your personal context, so it can comb through your emails, messages, and photos to find relevant information based on your query. It can then take action on your behalf, whether that's drafting an email in a specific tone or getting wine recommendations for a particular dish. Siri's voice is more expressive, but you can also customize the assistant's voice, its expressiveness, and its pace.

We've collated all the new things you can do with Siri AI if you want to try the revamped assistant.

Apple has focused on making iOS run faster in this update. The company says app launches are up to 30 percent faster, newly captured photos in your Photo Library load up to 70 percent faster, and AirDrop transfers are up to 80 percent faster. The iPhone will do a better job switching between Wi-Fi and cellular, so you hopefully won't have that awkward minute with no service while you wait for your device to switch networks as you leave the house. Many of these upgrades will affect older iPhone models, like the iPhone 11, thanks to a better-optimized CPU Scheduler.

Hate Liquid Glass? Love Liquid Glass? You have some options to make it work for your tastes in iOS 27. Apple says it has generally updated the design language to improve readability and contrast. App icons are sharper, for example. But you now finally have a slider in the Settings menu that lets you adjust the intensity of the Liquid Glass look, from super clear to more opaque. You can customize this in Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass.

Apple spent a lot of time in the WWDC keynote talking up child safety features in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27. A new Setup Assistant lets parents choose system apps and other essential apps for the child when first setting up an Apple device. An Ask to Browse feature means any new websites the kids encounter in Safari get sent to a parent for approval, and a feature called Communication Safety prevents children from seeing nudity or violence in the Messages or FaceTime apps; those are blurred by default.

Also new are Time Allowances and Schedules. Time Allowances let parents set an allotted amount of time kids can enjoy specific app categories (like Entertainment)—Apple has guidance on how much time makes sense based on the child's age. Schedules let parents choose what apps are available during different times of the week. All of this is also easier to view in a redesigned parental dashboard.

The Photos app is getting a small infusion of Apple Intelligence AI features, though remember that these features only work on iPhones that support Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro and newer).

The existing “Clean Up" feature—which lets you select objects in photos to remove (like a trash bag or people in the background)—now performs better thanks to Apple's upgraded foundation models. If the object you want to remove is larger, it will likely run through Apple's Private Cloud Compute servers for processing, but for smaller jobs, it will still handle the task on-device.

Extend is a new feature in the Photos app. This lets you expand a photo to add a little more to the edges—maybe you accidentally snapped a pic too close to a subject and want to give them some visual breathing room. It will generate what it thinks should be there based on the photo's context. (This feature works with Apple's diffusion model in the cloud.)

Finally, there's Spatial Reframing. This lets you alter a photo's perspective. Maybe you shot a little too high up and want to reframe the photo to make it look like you were crouching down further. The software will use generative AI to fill in the gaps after you change the perspective in the image (though Apple preserves faces and pets as much as possible to avoid altering them with fake pixels). You can read more about these features here.

Tap the Edit button on a photo and go to Tools to access the features in the Photos app. They're free features, but Apple sets usage limits, so you'll have to pay up for a higher-tier iCloud subscription if you want to use them more regularly.

Want to create AI slop? Apple has a more powerful image-generation model for its Image Playground app, meaning you can create higher-quality AI images in virtually any style—even photorealistic. The new version of Image Playground defaults to that photorealistic style if you don't specify a style in your prompt. These features have daily usage limits based on your iCloud subscription.

Similar to Google's Magic Cue on its Pixel phones, Apple is adding one-tap actions to Messages and Mail apps. If someone messages you about grabbing milk on the way home, you'll see a button to add it as a reminder. Or if someone asks about hanging out on a specific date, you'll see a Calendar button to create an event with one tap. These features were removed from the final version of iOS 27 but will be added in a future update.

Similarly, the Phone app now has a feature called Call Context. If you're on a call with Delta, for example, you'll see relevant flight information on the dialer screen, so you don't have to hunt in your email for a confirmation number during the call.

If you've ever tried to make a shortcut in Apple's Shortcuts app, you'll know it can be a little complicated. Now it’s getting easier. Instead of plugging in various rules and triggers, you can type what you want, and the Shortcuts app will understand your intent and set up an automated task for you. So you can naturally say, “Text my wife my ETA when I leave work,” and the Shortcuts app will set up an action that uses location services, Maps, traffic data, and Messages to automate a text message that fires off when you’re headed home.

Got a lot of tabs? Safari will now organize your many tabs into topics. Safari can also “notify” you when a web page changes, like a price drop or a restock.

Then there's Custom Extensions. This lets you describe a feature you want in Safari, and it will generate an extension. (It will first suggest existing third-party extensions that may be similar to what you're looking for.) For example, you can say, “When I hit the toolbar button on a recipe website, give me a button to save the recipe, add a star rating, and let me make comments; make the interface look nice.” Safari will generate the extension, and that's it. Extensions you make on one platform, like your iPhone, will carry over to your other devices, like your Mac.

You can read more about these Safari features here.

  • Better search in Apple Mail: Apple says a new ranking system will filter more relevant emails to the top of your search.
  • Easier Calendar event creation: You can use natural language to create a calendar event instead of filling out a bunch of fields. Type at the top, “Every Friday, make an event to water the plants,” and it'll make the event in a jiffy.
  • Dual Capture in FaceTime: You can now share video from your front and rear cameras at the same time during one-on-one calls.
  • Accessibility improvements: Apple’s VoiceOver accessibility mode has richer image descriptions, and there’s a new captioning feature that generates subtitles for any video you watch (kind of like Google's Live Transcribe), even translating them into other languages.
  • Maps upgrades: Flyover mode in Apple Maps lets you view a 3D map. Now, in iOS 27, Apple is combining aerial imagery with its Visual Intelligence models to render 3D models with far more detail. That means more detailed 3D buildings and trees.
  • Custom EQ with AirPods: AirPods are finally getting a custom equalizer, letting you customize the mids, lows, and highs in the AirPods settings menu.
  • Better iCloud Shared Albums: Android and Windows users can now more easily join iCloud Shared Albums and contribute their own photos. These albums also now support full-resolution images. You can now also create slideshows in the Photos app, save a video frame as a photo, and add star ratings to photos and videos to filter them.
  • Apple Health updates: The Health app now supports perimenopause and menopause, meaning the cycle-tracking feature can notify you when patterns suggest perimenopause.
  • Home app updates: If you have security cameras in your Apple Home app, you'll now receive smarter notifications that better describe what is happening around your home, much like Google and Amazon's richer notifications on their respective smart-home platforms.
  • Password fixes: If the Passwords app warns you about weak or compromised passwords, it can now automatically fix them for you.
  • Message syncing improvements: Apple says notifications for missed messages and unread count sync more quickly when you return to your iPad after some time.
